summary:
San Luis stands under the national framework: Argentina's Law 26.743, approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, and promulgated on 24 May 2012, allows a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval. An 'X' marker has been available on the national identity document (DNI) since 2021, and the United Nations described the statute as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region.

The operating position has narrowed through executive action rather than repeal of the statute. On 5 February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei published decree DNU 62/2025 amending Article 11 of the Gender Identity Law to bar under-18s from gender-affirming surgical and hormonal interventions, alongside decree DNU 61/2025 altering prison-sentencing law to change the placement of trans detainees. Both decrees apply nationally, to every province, and therefore bind San Luis.

Legal experts and LGBT+ organisations call both decrees unconstitutional and say that abruptly suspending adolescent treatments endangers trans youth; the decrees face judicial challenge. The outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

Trans activists report that the 2012 Gender Identity Law remains formally in force but is no longer guaranteed in practice. The Milei government eliminated the national Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry and dismissed trans hires made under the federal Trans Labor Quota Law, which reserves 1% of public-sector posts, and activists say the quota is no longer being implemented. Argentine trans activists interviewed by the Washington Blade on 10 April 2025 said the community faces a chaotic and desperate situation.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented high in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, a record, averaging one every 38 hours; Agencia Presentes reported the figures on 19 March 2026.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, but rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance, which an appeal court had removed in 2020. The gender-motivated-crime aggravator therefore does not apply in the case as it now stands.

An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration. Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws.
tangentialFactors:
Argentina's trajectory is the comparison point for the region: it legalised marriage equality in 2010, the first Latin American country to do so, and its 2012 gender identity statute was described by the United Nations as pioneering for the region. The Outright International overview of 12 March 2026 nonetheless records negative assessments on same-sex relations, gender recognition and organisation registration, a deterioration against that baseline.

The gap between statute and practice is the pattern most relevant to a visitor. The Gender Identity Law has not been repealed, yet activists told the Washington Blade on 10 April 2025 that it is no longer guaranteed, pointing to the elimination of the national Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry and to the non-implementation of the 1% federal Trans Labor Quota Law for public-sector posts.

Trans activists in Buenos Aires, interviewed on 4 April 2025, said the government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate; organisations named for Diana Sacayán, stabbed to death in 2015, and for Lohana Berkins were among those speaking. Buenos Aires is one data point within a national pattern of rising violence, not a measure of conditions in San Luis.

Nationally recorded hate crime reached at least 227 incidents based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025, a record averaging one every 38 hours, reported by Agencia Presentes on 19 March 2026 and described as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina.

outOfScopeNotes:
The judicial challenge to decrees DNU 62/2025 and DNU 61/2025 is unresolved in the sources available here; no ruling is recorded, so the decrees' continuing legal force is not settled.

No source in this inventory records enforcement of the Gender Identity Law, the prison-placement decree or the trans labor quota specifically within San Luis. Whether the quota is applied by San Luis provincial authorities, and how the province houses trans detainees, are not sourced.

The 2025 hate-crime total of at least 227 incidents is a national figure and is not broken down by province, so it does not indicate the level of violence in San Luis.

Whether the travesticidio aggravating circumstance is charged in other cases, or how provincial prosecutors in San Luis apply gender-motivated aggravation, is not covered by the sources here.
